subject: Dynamic occupancy model: Single yearly visit model

messages.author: 00ffce3d6ebe71e6
messages.subject: Dynamic occupancy model: Single yearly visit model
parts:
Hello,
I have been wondering whether fitting a multiyear dynamic occupancy model makes any sense when I only have 1 sampling occasion within each year?
In this example, there are 67 sites that were visited once a year over 41 years and I want to investigate the extinction and colonization patterns.
I know that the colext function lets me fit this kind of model, but I was wondering whether it is actually doing what I think it is.

67 sites
Maximum number of observations per site: 41 
Mean number of observations per site: 41 
Number of primary survey periods: 41 
Number of secondary survey periods: 1 
Sites with at least one detection: 63 

Tabulation of y observations:
   0    1 
2279  468 

Thanks

Robby

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Dynamic occupancy model: Single yearly visit model
parts:
Hi Robby,

you can of course do this but must know that your estimates you get will be biased if detection probability p < 1 and if there are patterns in p in time and/or space. However, since it seems to me that in a majority of analyses in ecology, people still ignore p, I think you can do this, too, or at least, this should not be seen as a fatal flaw when you want to publish this. If this is all the data you have, then why not use it, but discuss very carefully the potential for the violation of the p<1 and the p = constant assumptions to fault the main inferences you make about your system.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Dynamic occupancy model: Single yearly visit model
parts:
hi Robby,
 you can in fact fit a multi-year occupancy model when there is only 1 replicate per primary occasion -- see this paper here:
Peach, M.A., Cohen, J.B. and Frair, J.L., 2017. Single‐visit dynamic occupancy models: an approach to account for imperfect detection with Atlas data. Journal of applied ecology, 54(6), pp.2033-2042.
 (and probably some others too). 
regards
andy

Yes, these authors describe a model where you actually estimate p even in this situation.
Plus, there is also the little-known "brother" of the famous Dail-Madsen model for abundance (2011), the almost unknown Dail-Madsen model for occupancy (2013): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23006066

Best regards  -- Marc
